The Moroccan spadefoot, Pelobates varaldii, displays distinct morphological dimorphism between the sexes, with field surveys indicating that adult females attain a maximum snout–vent length of 7.0 centimeters [Li = 7.0 centimeters], whereas males typically reach a slightly smaller ultimate size of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters]. This difference in body length correlates with distinct differences in adult body mass; gravid females achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 39.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 39.6 grams], reflecting the considerable energetic investment in oocyte production, while adult males reach an ultimate wet weight of about 31.4 grams [Wwi = about 31.4 grams]. The species exhibits a comparatively rapid early development; embryos incubated at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] hatch after just 7 days [ab = 7 days], a short embryonic period consistent with the ephemeral nature of the temporary pools this species typically exploits. This rapid embryogenesis is followed by an extended larval phase that culminates in metamorphosis.

Following eclosion, the small, yolk-dependent larva, which initially weighs only about 0.0031 grams [Wwb = about 0.0031 grams], embarks on a period of rapid growth. Tadpoles develop through a series of distinct Gosner stages in the warm, shallow waters of temporary ponds, where they graze on algae and detritus. Based on comparative data from closely related spadefoot species, the maximum daily reproductive rate under stable conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is estimated to be approximately 4.3 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4.3 eggs per day]. This estimate is derived from integrating the size of individual clutches with the frequency of spawning events across a breeding season. Females typically produce a single clutch of several thousand eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = several thousand eggs per spawning event], and they may deposit up to two such clutches each year [F_R_i = up to two such clutches each year] during the brief rainy season, which can extend from November to March depending on the timing and intensity of autumnal rains. This relatively extended lifespan for a small anuran allows individuals multiple breeding opportunities across several seasons, which is a critical life-history buffer against years of reproductive failure caused by drought. The species' fossorial habits, spending the majority of the year buried in sandy soils, likely contribute to this longevity by reducing predation risk and metabolic demands. Field studies have documented individuals surviving for over a decade in protected habitats, although the harsh conditions of the Moroccan climate often mean that the average lifespan in highly disturbed or marginal sites is considerably shorter.

The interplay between developmental rates and environmental temperature is a critical determinant of population dynamics in this species. The exceptionally short incubation period of 7 days [ab = 7 days] at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], combined with a larval period that can last several months, illustrates a finely tuned balance between rapid hatching and the need for substantial juvenile growth. This life history, combining high fecundity with an extended longevity and delayed maturity, is emblematic of a species adapted to the stochastic rainfall patterns of Mediterranean temporary wetlands.
